text: Hector Returns to Battle: He Is Willing to Die for Glory, but Have His Wife and Child Chosen That Cost?
When Hector returns to Troy, he does not find his wife at home.
A servant tells him that Andromache has heard the Greeks are drawing near and has hurried to the walls carrying their child.
So Hector crosses the streets again and makes his way to the Scaean Gate.
This is the very place from which he is preparing to return to battle.
Andromache comes from the city.
Hector comes back from the battlefield.
They meet before the gate, where one direction leads home and the other to war.
Their infant son is in his nurse's arms.
At the sight of the child, Hector smiles without a word.
But Andromache takes his hand and says through her tears:
Your courage will kill you.
This farewell is often told as follows:
A hero chooses between love for his family and his duty to the city.
Andromache asks him to stay.
Hector returns to battle to defend Troy.
There is nothing wrong with that summary.
But it makes Andromache's request seem simpler than it is in the text.
She does not merely say:
Do not fight. Stay home with me.
She begins by recounting her past.
Achilles has killed her father.
Her seven brothers died on the same day.
Her mother was ransomed, but she too later died.
And so she says:
Hector is now her father and mother, her brother and her husband.
If he dies, she will not merely be losing her partner in marriage.
The whole world of kinship that the war has left her will disappear with him.
Then she makes a specific proposal:
Do not keep fighting in the most dangerous part of the front line.
Position the army near the fig tree.
That is a vulnerable point in the walls, where the bravest Greek warriors have already tried several times to break through.
She is not asking Troy to stop resisting.
She is proposing another way to resist.
This also requires us to read Hector's reply more precisely.
He says:
I have thought about all these things too.
But if he were to avoid battle like a coward, he would be ashamed before the men of Troy, and before its women as well.
He has learned always to be brave, to fight at the very front of the Trojan ranks, and to win glory for his father and himself.
Hector does not merely say:
The city needs me.
He brings several things together:
Protecting Troy.
Standing at the front.
Not being seen as a coward.
Continuing to be the warrior he has always been.
Winning glory for his family and himself.
These reasons support one another, but they are not the same thing.
A person can take on a public responsibility.
There need not be only one action that counts as truly fulfilling it.
What Andromache proposes is precisely a possibility that would still defend the city without singling Hector out for the most dangerous position.
The text does not prove that her tactics would necessarily be better.
But her presence at least prevents us from simply equating “returning to the very front” with “defending Troy” itself.
Nor should Hector's shame be lightly mocked.
An army under siege needs its soldiers to trust that they will not abandon one another in danger.
If its most important commander stays inside the walls, others may think he is leaving ordinary soldiers to bear the risk.
A hero's reputation does more than satisfy him personally.
It can also sustain morale, order, and trust in a shared defense.
If everyone withdrew for the sake of their family, the families inside Troy might be destroyed all the sooner.
So Andromache's tears do not lead directly to the conclusion:
Hector should stay at home.
Nor does his concern about what others think mean that all his public reasons are really just vanity.
In his world, shame and glory do help sustain the community.
The question is:
Does a form of judgment that has real force thereby acquire the final say over every action?
Hector goes on to say something more disturbing.
He knows that Troy will one day fall.
Priam will die.
The people will suffer disaster.
Yet of all these future sorrows, what he finds most unbearable is Andromache being carried off by a Greek warrior.
She will weave and draw water in another land, deprived of her freedom.
Someone will point to her and say:
Look, that is Hector's wife. Hector was once the bravest warrior in Troy.
Those words will renew her grief, because Hector will no longer be there to protect her from slavery.
Finally, he says:
May he already lie buried in the earth before he hears her crying as she is dragged away.
This passage shows that Hector is not blind to what his wife will have to bear.
He sees it very clearly.
He even describes her captivity as a future that pains him more than the deaths of his parents, his brothers, and the whole city.
Yet he still chooses to return to battle.
This is not necessarily a contradiction.
Perhaps he believes that he must keep fighting precisely because Andromache will be enslaved if the city falls.
If its strongest defender steps back now, that day may arrive sooner.
For him, returning to battle both pursues glory and protects his wife and child.
The problem is:
He has chosen a way of protecting them that depends on his continuing to live and continuing to win.
If he falls in battle, his wife and child will bear the most immediate consequences of that choice.
Someone may be willing to defend others with his life.
But when his death also deprives those he protects of their only support, the sacrifice no longer belongs to him alone.
Hector can say:
I am willing to die for Troy.
Andromache, however, must live in a world where “Hector has died for Troy.”
So must their child.
They have not made the same decision, but that will not spare them its cost.
This does not mean that his wife and child have an absolute veto over Hector's public duties.
Entering an intimate relationship does not mean that from then on a person may do only what their family considers safe.
Soldiers, doctors, rescuers, rulers, and many others in public roles may face real danger.
If being loved means that one can no longer take risks, love becomes another form of possession.
Andromache cannot make the safety of everyone else in Troy cease to matter merely by saying, “You matter most to me.”
Conversely, Hector cannot treat the future of his wife and child as a private cost of his own merely by saying, “This is the glory I am willing to bear.”
Both these limits must hold at once.
A person's family cannot own every direction their life might take.
Nor can that person pretend to be the only one who pays for the direction they choose.
As his father reaches out to him, the infant suddenly begins to cry.
He is frightened by the bronze of Hector's helmet and its horsehair crest swaying in the wind.
His father and mother laugh together.
Hector takes off his helmet and sets it on the ground.
For a moment, the hero of the battlefield becomes a father his child can approach again.
He lifts his son, kisses him, and prays to the gods:
May this child one day be outstanding among the Trojans, as Hector himself is.
May he be braver and stronger than his father.
May people one day see him returning from battle with the bloodstained spoils of an enemy he has killed and say:
He is far greater than his father.
May this make his mother rejoice.
The prayer is tender and cruel at once.
Holding a child whom his helmet has just frightened into tears, Hector wishes that he will one day enter the same system of warrior glory.
What the mother fears most at this moment is her husband's death in battle.
Yet the father hopes that their son will one day bring his mother joy through victories on the battlefield too.
This is not because Hector does not love his child.
It is precisely out of love that he offers the child what he believes to be the best possible future.
In his world, martial courage, defending the city, surpassing one's father, and winning honor are the most worthy things a boy can aspire to.
Parents often bless their children this way.
They hope their children will possess the abilities they prize most.
Accomplish what they themselves could not.
Even do better than they did.
But a blessing can also place one generation's values directly into the next generation's future.
The child cannot yet answer.
Nor have his mother's tears changed the language of this prayer.
Hector has not ordered his son to become a warrior.
But for someone who cannot yet speak, he has already pictured the kind of life most deserving of praise.
This love is real.
It must still wait for the child's own answer in the years to come.
Andromache takes the child, smiling through her tears.
Hector touches her tenderly.
He says that no one can send him to Hades before his appointed time; once fate arrives, neither coward nor brave man can escape it.
Then he tells his wife to return to her loom and servants, saying that war is the business of men, and among the men of Troy, his above all.
The language of fate makes the decision seem already beyond the individual.
Since no one can escape their destined death, a brave man should not abandon his post for fear of dying.
There is real force in this.
But “death will come in the end” cannot by itself decide:
Where one should stand now.
What kind of defense to adopt.
Who should share the risk.
Finitude does not supply a single answer about how to act.
That cowards and brave men alike will die does not make every way of taking risks the same.
Hector picks up his helmet and heads back toward the battlefield.
Andromache returns home, looking back as she goes.
Her maids gather around her.
Hector is still alive, yet they have already begun to mourn him.
This ending does not say:
Hector's choice must be wrong.
Nor does it say:
The hero's duty has already fully accounted for his wife's sorrow.
It brings two different times into the same moment.
For Hector, the fighting is not over. He can still keep defending the city and keep coming back.
For the women at home, a future death has already entered the present.
Others do not begin to bear the hero's decision only when he finally falls.
The moment he puts his helmet back on, it has already entered the lives of his wife and child.
Should Hector, then, have stayed?
The work offers its readers no answer without loss.
Staying might put the city in greater danger, and might leave other warriors to bear the share that should have been his.
Returning to the front might save Troy, or it might deprive the entire city of its most important defender.
Andromache's plan might be more prudent, or it might fail to replace the role Hector plays at the front.
We do not know.
What we can establish is not which set of tactics must be right.
It is this:
“I am willing to die” is never the whole reckoning in a public action.
This is true of an ordinary soldier.
It is true of a father.
It is all the more true of the hero on whom a community most depends.
Through many relationships, his life has already become a condition of other people's futures.
Hector's greatness does not disappear because of this.
He sees the danger and is still willing to return.
He knows he may fail and still refuses to leave others to defend the city alone.
That is why the epic sings of him.
But singing of a hero does not require his values to monopolize the entire scene.
Andromache sees the war too.
She is not asking from the safety of her home for others to bear the burden in her place.
War has already taken her entire birth family, and she describes precisely the next loss that she and her child will have to bear.
Hector stands for public duty.
She does not stand merely for private weakness.
Both are speaking about Troy's future.
From different positions, they see who will have to bear that future.
A hero has the right to decide what he is willing to risk himself for.
His public role may also require him to face real danger.
But when glory, duty, and personal identity are tightly bound together, someone should still keep asking:
Is this truly the only way to fulfill that duty?
If the action fails, who will live with the consequences?
Have those people already been made part of the decision, rather than merely people who deserve sympathy after the hero's death?
Andromache does not win the argument.
Hector still returns to battle.
But the epic lets her finish giving her reasons before the city gate.
From that moment on, Hector's departure for war can no longer be written simply as one man's willingness to pay for glory with his life.
His wife and child have been drawn into the cost as well.
And at that same moment, they have not expressed the same willingness.

*Textual basis: Homer, Iliad, Book 6, focusing on Hector's meeting with Andromache and their infant son at the Scaean Gate (approximately 6.369–413); Andromache's account of losing her father, seven brothers, and mother, and her proposal to position troops near the fig tree at a vulnerable point in the walls (approximately 6.414–439); Hector's reasons for returning, invoking shame before the Trojan men and women, his accustomed place at the front of the fighting, and glory for his father and himself, followed by his vision of Troy's fall and his wife's captivity (approximately 6.440–465); the child's fear of the helmet, Hector's removal of it as he takes his son in his arms, and his prayer that the boy will be braver and bring home bloodstained spoils (approximately 6.466–481); and the women of the household mourning Hector while he is still alive after Andromache returns home (approximately 6.482–502). This essay does not portray Andromache as asking her husband to evade public responsibility, nor does it equate Hector's public responsibility with the justification of every particular heroic action.*
